translations.text: After Ahab died, Moab rebelled.

Ahaziah became ill and lay in his upper room in Samaria. He sent messengers and told them, “Go and inquire for me of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this illness.” So they went to inquire for him.

The angel of the Lord called Elijah the Tishbite and said to him, “Get up, go and meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and tell them, ‘Is there no God of Israel, that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? That is not so!’”
“This is what the Lord says: ‘You will not rise from the bed on which you are lying. You will certainly die there.’” Elijah went and told them this.
His messengers returned to him, and he said to them, “What brought you back?”

They told him, “A man met us and said to us, ‘Go back to the king who sent you and tell him: This is what the Lord says: Is there no God of Israel, that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? That is not so! You will not rise from the bed on which you are lying. You will certainly die.’”
He said to them, “What did the man who met you and told you this message look like?”
They told him, “The man was hairy and had a leather belt around his waist.” He said to them, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”
He sent fifty men with their captain to summon him. They went to him and found him sitting on top of a hill. Their captain said to him, “Man of God, the king summons you. Come down!”

Elijah answered their captain, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and the fifty men with you.” Fire came down from heaven and consumed him and the fifty men with him.
The king again sent fifty men with their captain. Their captain called to him and said, “Man of God, the king summons you. Come down quickly!”
Elijah answered him, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and the fifty men with you.” Fire came down from heaven and consumed him and the fifty men with him.

Once again, for a third time, the king sent fifty men with their captain. This third captain went to him, knelt before Elijah, and said to him, “Man of God, I beg you, let my life and the lives of your servants be precious in your sight.
Look, fire came down from heaven and consumed the first two captains and their fifty men each. But now, let my life be precious in your sight.”
The angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah and said to him, “Go down with him, and do not be afraid of them.” Elijah got up, went down with him, and went to the king.

Elijah spoke to him and said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Why did he send to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? That is not so! You will not rise from the bed on which you are lying, for you will certainly die.’”
He died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken to him.
All the affairs of Ahaziah and everything he did are written in the book of their prophets, the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

Joram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned for twelve years. He did evil before the Lord, but not like his brother or his mother. He removed the images of Baal that his father had made and broke them. Yet he followed the sin of the house of Jeroboam, who had led Israel into sin, and did not abandon it. The Lord’s anger was stirred up against the house of Ahab.
Then, when God was about to take Elijah up into heaven, Elijah and Elisha went from Jericho.
Elijah said to Elisha, “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me to Bethel.” Elisha said to Elijah, “As the Lord lives and as you live, I will not leave you.” And he reached Bethel.
The members of the prophetic company in Bethel came to Elisha and said to him, “Do you know that today the Lord will take your master away from over your head?” He said to them, “I know. Be silent.”
Elijah said to Elisha, “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me to Jericho.” Elisha said to him, “As the Lord lives and as you live, I will not leave you.” And they reached Jericho.
The members of the prophetic company in Jericho came to Elisha and said to him, “Do you know that today the Lord will take your master away from over your head?” He said to them, “I know. Be silent.”
Elijah said to Elisha, “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me toward the Jordan.” Elisha said to him, “As the Lord lives and as you live, I will not leave you.” And the two of them went on.
Fifty men from the prophetic company were with them and stood facing them at a distance, while the two of them stood beside the Jordan.
Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the water of the Jordan. The water stood on either side, and the two of them crossed over and stood on dry ground after coming out.

After this, when the two of them had crossed over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask me what you want me to do for you before I am taken up from you.” Elisha said to Elijah, “Let a double portion of the Holy Spirit that is upon you be upon me.”
Elijah said to him, “You have asked for a difficult thing. Nevertheless, if you see me as I am taken up from you, it will be so for you. But if you do not see me, it will not be so for you.”
While the two of them were walking and talking, a chariot of fire and horses of fire came between them and separated them. Elijah went up as though in a whirlwind and as though into heaven.
Elisha saw him and said to him, “Father, father! The might of Israel and their strength!” After this he saw him no more. He tore his clothes into two pieces.
Elijah let his cloak fall down to him, and it fell upon Elisha’s head. Elisha returned and stood on the bank of the Jordan.

He took Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from above his head, and struck the water with it, but it refused to divide. He said, “Where is Elijah’s God? And how?” Then he struck the water, and it divided and stood on either side, and Elisha crossed over.

The sons of the prophets who were in Jericho saw him coming toward them and said, “The Holy Spirit that was upon Elijah has come upon Elisha.” They went to meet him and bowed down to the ground before him.

They said to him, “Look, here with your servants are fifty strong men. Let them go and search for your master. Perhaps the Spirit of the Lord has taken him and set him down in the Jordan, or on one of the mountains, or in one of the valleys.” Elisha said to them, “Do not send them.”
They pressed him until he was ashamed before them. They sent fifty men, who searched for three days but did not find him.
Elisha was staying in Jericho. Elisha said to them, “Did I not tell you, ‘Do not send them, and do not go’?”
The people of that city said to Elisha, “Look, the location of this city is good, as God sees, but the water of the region is bad, and the women are barren.”
Elisha said to them, “Bring me a new bowl and put salt in it.” They brought it to him.
Elisha went to the spring of water, threw the salt into it, and said, “This is what the Lord says: I have healed this water, so that no one will die from it or become barren because of it.”
From that time the water has remained healed to this day, just as Elisha said.
He went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up along the road, he encountered young boys coming out of the city. They began mocking him and said to him, “Go up, go up, bald man!”
When he turned around and saw them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord. Then two bears came out of the wilderness and killed forty-two of the boys.
From there he went to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.
Joram son of Ahab became king over Israel in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned for twelve years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, though not like his father or his mother. He tore down the image of Baal that his father had made.
Nevertheless, he followed the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel astray, and he did not abandon it.
Mesha, king of Moab, [?] the city of Menokth, gave him a hundred thousand wool-bearing sheep and a hundred thousand [?] young goats.
After Ahab died, Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
At that time King Joram went out from Samaria and mobilized Israel.

He went and sent a message to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, saying, “The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you come with me to fight against Moab?” He said to him, “Yes, I will go up with you. I am as you are, and you are as I am. My people are as your people, and my horses are as your horses.”
He said to him, “By which road shall we go up?” He replied, “By the road through the wilderness of Edom.”
The king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom set out. They traveled around for seven days, and they ran out of water for the army and their pack animals.
The king of Israel said, “Alas for us! Has the Lord brought us three kings here to deliver us into the hands of Moab?”

Jehoshaphat said, “Is there no prophet of God here, through whom we may inquire about God’s word?” One of the king of Israel’s servants answered, “Elisha son of Shaphat is here, who [?] Elijah’s hands.”
Jehoshaphat said, “Is the word of the Lord with him?” So the king of Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and the king of Edom went down to him.

Elisha said to the king of Israel, “What have I to do with you? Go to your father’s prophets.” The king of Israel said, “Has the Lord brought us three kings here to deliver us into the hands of Moab?”
Elisha said to them, “As the Lord, the God of hosts, lives, before whom I stand, if I did not respect Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not even look.”
“Now bring me a musician.” Then, when the musician played, the hand of the Lord came upon him.
He said, “This is what the Lord says: Dig pits in this riverbed.
For this is what the Lord says: Though you see no wind and see no rain, this riverbed will fill, and you, your livestock, and your animals will drink.
This is an easy thing in the eyes of the Lord. He will also deliver Moab into your hands.
Destroy all their great cities, cut down all their good trees, stop up all their springs of water, and smash all their fine property with stones.”
When morning dawned over the land, at the time when the sacrifice was offered, water came from the direction of Edom, and that whole land filled with water.

When all the Moabites heard that these kings had come up to fight them, they raised a cry throughout all their districts, saying, “Come to help, all of you, with your farming tools!” They gathered and stood on the mountaintop.
They rose early in the morning, and when the sun shone on that water, the Moabites saw the water before them red like blood.
He said to him, “These kings have fought among themselves. This is blood from battle! They have killed one another. Now let us go down and plunder them!”
They entered the camp of Israel, and the Israelites rose up and struck down the Moabites. The Moabites fled before the Israelites, who advanced and continued striking down the Moabites as they went.

They demolished five of their cities. All the men of Israel threw stones into all their good fields and filled them. They stopped up all their pits and cut down all their good trees and plants. They demolished the wall of their city, and the slingers surrounded them and struck them down.
When the king of Moab saw that they were slaughtering his people, and saw that they had defeated them, he took seven hundred men with him and went to fight the king of Edom, but he could not.
Then he took his firstborn son, who was to reign in his place, and sacrificed him on top of the wall. The Israelites felt deep remorse, and they departed and returned to their own land.

A woman from among the families of the prophets cried out to Elisha and said, “Your servant, who feared the Lord, was my husband, and he has died. Now the creditor has come to take my two children and make them his slaves.”

Elisha said to her, “What do you want me to do for you? Tell me, what do you have in your house?” She said to him, “Your servant has nothing at all in her house except a jar of oil with which I anoint myself.”
He said to her, “Go and borrow earthenware vessels from your neighbors.
Go into your house and shut your door behind you and your children. Pour into those earthenware vessels, and set aside each one that is full.”
She entered her house and shut the door behind herself and her children. They brought the vessels to her, and she poured.
She said to her children, “Bring me more earthenware vessels.” They said to her, “All the earthenware vessels have been used.” Then the oil stopped.
She went and told the man of God. Elisha said to her, “Go, sell it, pay your debt, and provide food as well. Support yourself and your children [?] with the oil that remains.”
Then one day Elisha passed through Shunem. A prominent woman lived there, and she persuaded him to stay and eat, for [?] he passed that way. He would stop there to eat.
The woman said to her husband, “This is a holy man of God who continually passes our way.”
“Let us make him one small upstairs room, and put a bed, a chair, a lampstand, and a table there for him. Whenever he passes our way, he can stay there.”
Then one day he went there and spent the night in the upper room.
He said to Gehazi, his attendant, “Call this Shunammite woman for me.” He called her, and she stood before him.

He said to him, “Tell her, ‘Look, you have shown me all this honor. What can I do for you? Do you have any concern to bring before the king or the messenger?’” She answered him, “I live here among my own people.”
He said, “What shall we do for her?” Gehazi, his attendant, said to him, “She is a teacher, for she has no children, and her husband is old.”
He called her, and she stood at the doorway.
Elisha said to her, “A year from today, while you are alive, you will have a son.” She said to him, “My lord, do not lie to your servant.”
Then the woman conceived and bore a son a year later, while she was alive, on the day Elisha had told her.
The child grew up and went out to his father in the harvest field.
He said to his father, “My head! My head!” His father said to his servant, “Take him to his mother.”
She laid him in her lap, on her knees, until noon.
Then, when he died, she carried him upstairs and laid him on the bed of the man of God. She shut the door on him and went out.
She called her husband and said to him, “Call and send me one of the servants and one donkey, so that I can go to the man of God and return.”
He said to her, “Why are you going to him today, when it is neither the new moon nor the Sabbath?” She said, “To greet him.”
They saddled a donkey for her, and she said to her servant, “Get up, let us go. Do not slow my journey unless I tell you. Come, follow me, and let us go to the man of God on Mount Carmel.”
When Elisha saw the woman coming, he said to Gehazi his servant, “Look, there is the Shunammite woman.”
“Run now to meet her and say to her, ‘Peace to you! Is your husband well? Is your child well?’” She said to him, “All is well.”

She reached Elisha on the mountain and took hold of his feet. Gehazi came to stop her, but Elisha said to him, “Leave her alone, for her soul is distressed. The LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.”
She said to him, “Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not tell you, ‘Do not lie to me’?”

Elisha said to Gehazi, “Tie up your clothing around your waist, take my staff and carry it in your hand, and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him. Lay my staff on the child's face.”
The child's mother said to him, “As the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you.” So Elisha got up and went with her.
Gehazi went ahead of them and arrived first. He laid the staff on the child’s face, but the child neither spoke nor heard. He went back, met him, and reported to him, “The child has not awakened.”
Elisha entered the house and found the child dead, lying on the bed.
Elisha went into the house, shut the door on the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.
He climbed up and lay on the child, placing his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He lay upon him, and the child's body became warm.
He got up and walked back and forth in the house. Then he went up again and lay upon the child. He did this seven times, and afterward the child opened his eyes.
Elisha called Gehazi and said to him, “Call this Shunammite woman.” He called her, and she came to him. Elisha said to her, “Here is your son; take him.”
The woman came in and bowed to him, prostrating herself at his feet. She took her child and went out.

Elisha returned to the region of Gilgal, and there was a famine in the land. The disciples of the prophets came and sat before him. Elisha said to his servant, “Heat a large pot and cook stew for the disciples of the prophets.”

He went out into the countryside to gather greens from the ground and found a vineyard in the countryside. He entered it and gathered greens there, filling his garment. He put them into the pot and cooked them, not knowing what was in it.
Then he served it to them to eat. When they ate the stew, they all cried out together and said, “There is poison in this pot, man of God!” They could not eat it.
Elisha said, “Bring flour and put it into the pot.” Elisha said to Gehazi, “Serve it to the people so that they may eat.” After that, nothing harmful was found in the pot.
A man came from Sarira and brought the man of God twenty barley loaves from the first fruits of his grain and two [?]. He said to his servant, “Give these to the men so that they may eat.”

His servant said to him, “How can I serve these to a hundred men?” He said to him, “Serve them to the people so that they may eat, for this is what the LORD says: ‘They will eat and have some left over.’”
They ate and had some left over, as the Lord had said.

Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, was a great man in his master's eyes and was honored. His master esteemed him because the Lord had delivered the Syrians through him. He was a strong and mighty man, but leprosy had afflicted him.
When he came with the Syrians to fight, he took captive a young girl from the land of Israel and placed her with his wife.
She said to her mistress, “My master should go to the man of God, the prophet who is in Samaria, and he will cure him of this leprosy.”
His wife went in to him and told him, saying, “This is what the girl from the land of Israel said.”

The king of Syria said to Naaman, “Come, go! I will send a letter for you to the king of Israel.” He went and took with him ten talents of silver, eight hundred pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing.
He delivered the letter to the king of Israel. The letter said, “Now, when this letter reaches you, look: I have sent my servant Naaman to you. Cure him of his leprosy.”

When the king of Israel read that letter, he tore his clothes and said, “Am I God, able to kill and bring to life, that he sends this man with leprosy to me for me to cure him of his leprosy? Look and see how this man is seeking a pretext against us!”

When Elisha heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent a message to the king, saying, “Why have you torn your clothes? Let Naaman come to me, and you will know that there is a prophet in Israel.”
Naaman went with horses and chariots and stood at the doorway of Elisha's house.
Elisha sent a message to him, saying, “Go, immerse yourself seven times in the Jordan River. The appearance of your flesh will be restored, and you will be healed of your leprosy.”
Naaman became angry and went away, saying, “I thought that he would come out and stand beside me, call on the name of the Lord his God, lay his hands on me, and heal me.

“Are not the waters of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel? The River Abana and the River Pharpar are better! Could I not go and wash in them and be healed of my leprosy?” He turned away and went off in anger.
His servants came to him and said, “The prophet has told you a great thing. Do as he told you: go, wash, and be healed.”
Naaman went down and immersed himself seven times in the Jordan River, as Elisha had told him. He was healed, and his flesh became like the flesh of a little child.

He returned to Elisha with his entire company. He came to him, stood before him, and said, “Now I know that there is no God anywhere on earth except in Israel. Now, please accept a gift from the hand of your servant.”
Elisha said to him, “As God lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” He urged him to accept it, but he would not agree.

Naaman said to him, “If not, let your servant be given an omer measure, a load for two mules, for from now on your servant will offer sacrifices to no other gods, but to the Lord alone, according to your word.

“May the Lord forgive your servant in this matter: when my master enters the temple of Rimmon to bow down to him there, he leans on my hand, and I too bow down with him in the temple of Rimmon. When he bows down in the temple of Rimmon, may the Lord forgive your servant for this.”
Elisha said to Naaman, “Return, then, in peace.” He departed from him in peace for his own country, Deblathah.
Gehazi, Elisha's servant, said, “Look, my master has spared this Syrian Naaman and has taken nothing from what he brought him. As the Lord lives, I will run after him and take something from him.”
Gehazi pursued Naaman and followed him. Naaman turned and saw him following behind him. He got down from his chariot, went back, and met him.

He said to him, “Peace to you! My master has sent me to you and says to you, ‘Two men from the company of the prophets have come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.’”
Naaman said to him, “Take two talents.” He took them and put them in two bags, along with two changes of clothing. He had two of his servants carry them for him, and they went ahead of him.
They went into the darkness. Then he received it from them, brought it into his house, and sent those men away.
Then he went in and stood before his master. Elisha said to Gehazi, “Where have you come from?” Gehazi said to him, “Your servant has not gone anywhere at all.”

Elisha said to him, “Did my heart not go with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Now you have taken gold, and now you have taken clothes, so that you may have vineyards, [?] gardens, olive groves, cattle, sheep, male slaves, and female slaves.”
“But Naaman’s leprosy will come upon you and your descendants forever.” At that moment Naaman’s leprosy seized Gehazi, and Gehazi left Elisha’s presence with his whole body leprous, white as snow.
The disciples of the prophets said to Elisha, “Look, this dwelling where we live under your guidance is too cramped for us.”
“Let us go toward the Jordan and cut a log for ourselves there, and make ourselves a dwelling there where we can live.” He said to them, “Go.”
One of them said to him, “Please come with your servants.” He answered, “Yes, I too will come.”
He went with them, and they reached the Jordan River and cut down trees.
While one of them was cutting a log, his axe head came loose and fell into the water. He clutched his head and cried out, saying, “My lord! And this one was concealed!”
The man of God said to him, “Where did it fall?” He showed him where it had fallen. He stripped off a piece of tree bark and threw it there, and the iron axe head floated.
He said, “Pick it up! Here is your tool.” He lowered his hand and picked it up.
The king of Syria waged war against Israel. He consulted with his attendants and said to them, “We will camp in the region of Phelmon.”
Elisha sent word to the king of Israel, saying, “Be careful not to go into that region, because the Syrians are hiding there.”
The king of Israel sent men to guard for him the place Elisha had told him about, once and then again.
The king of Syria was deeply troubled by this matter. He called his attendants and said to them, “Will you not tell me who is informing the king of Israel?”
One of his attendants said to him, “My lord, is it not Elisha, the prophet in Israel? He tells the king of Israel all your words and everything you say in the upper room of your house.”
He said to them, “Go and find out where he is, and I will send men to bring him.” They told him, “He is in Dothan.”
He sent horses, chariots, and troops there. They arrived there at night and surrounded the city.
Elisha’s young servant woke up, got up, and went outside. He saw an army surrounding the city, with horses and chariots. His servant said to him, “My lord, what shall we do?”
Elisha said to him, “Do not be afraid. Those who are with us are more numerous than they are.”
Elisha prayed and said, “Lord, open this young man’s eyes so that he may see.” The Lord opened his eyes, and he saw horses and chariots of fire all over the mountain, surrounding Elisha.
They came down to Elisha. Elisha prayed to the Lord and said, “Lord, make these people blind.” He made them blind, just as Elisha had said.
Elisha said to them, “This is not the city, and this is not the road. Come, follow me, and I will take you to the man you are looking for.” He took them and led them to the city of Samaria.
Elisha said, “Lord, open their eyes so that they may see.” He opened their eyes, and they saw and realized that they were in the middle of Samaria.
When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, “Shall I kill them, my father?”

He said to him, “Do not kill them, since you did not capture them with your spear or your bow. Rather, it is those you captured with your spear and your bow that you kill. Set food and water before them so that they may eat and drink and return to their master.”
He set [?] before them, and they ate and drank. He sent them away, and they returned to their master. The Syrians did not again wage war against the land of Israel.
After this, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered all his forces, went and besieged Samaria, and remained there.
There was a severe famine in Samaria. The Syrians continued their siege until a donkey’s head cost fifty shekels of silver, and a quarter of a kab measure of dove dung cost fifty shekels of silver.
As the king of Israel was walking along the roof and going around the wall, a woman cried out and said to him, “Help me, my lord, king of Israel!”
He said to her, “If the Lord does not save you, where can I get help to save you? From the winepress or from the grainfield?”
The king said to her, “What is the matter with you?” She said to him, “This woman said to me, ‘Bring your son so that we can eat him today.’”
“We cooked my son and ate him. Then, on the next day, I said to her, ‘Bring your son too, so that we may eat him.’ But she hid her son.”
When the king heard what the woman said to him, he tore his clothes as he walked along the top of the wall. The people saw the sackcloth that the king wore next to his skin underneath his clothes.
He said, “May God do this to me, and may he kill me, if Elisha’s head remains on his neck today!”

Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. The king sent a man from among those who stood before him. Before the man whom the king had sent reached him, Elisha said to the elders, “Do you realize that this murderer’s son has sent someone to cut off my head? Watch for his arrival, shut the door, bar it, and leave him standing at the door, for the sound of my lord’s footsteps is behind him.”
While he was speaking with them, the man whom the king had sent arrived and came down to him. Elisha said, “Look, this calamity has come upon me from the Lord. Why, then, should I wait for the Lord?”

Elisha said to him, “Listen to the word of the Lord. This is what the Lord says: Tomorrow at this time, a measure of wheat will cost a shekel, and two measures of barley will be sold for a shekel at the gate of Samaria.”

The man on whose arm the king leaned answered Elisha, “Even if the Lord made streams of grain flow from heaven, what you say would not happen.” Elisha said to him, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not taste it.”
There were four men with leprosy at the city gate. They said to one another, “Why should we sit here until we die?”

“If we enter the city, we will die of hunger there, because the city is starving. If we stay here, we will die. So now, come, let us go into the Syrian camp. If they spare our lives, we will live; if they kill us, we will die.”
They got up in the darkness and entered the Syrian camp. When they reached the Syrians, they found no one there.

For the Lord had made the Syrian camp hear the sound of chariots, the sound of horses, and the sound of a large army. The Syrians said to one another, “Now the king of Israel has hired the king of the Hittites and the king of Egypt against us, to come down upon us.”
They panicked, got up, and fled in the darkness. They left their camp, their horses, and their donkeys just as they were, and escaped for their lives.

The men with leprosy entered the camp and went into a tent. They ate and drank, took gold, silver, and clothes from there, and went away. They entered another camp, took things from there too, and went away and hid them.
They said to one another, “What we are doing is not right. This is a blessed day. If we remain silent and wait until morning, we will be guilty. Come now, let us go and tell the king’s household.”

They went and called out at the city gate, reporting, “We entered the Syrian camp, and we found no one there. There was no sound of anyone there, only horses and donkeys, and their camp remained just as it was.”
The messengers went inside and told the king’s household.

The king got up in the night and said to his servants, “Let me tell you what the Syrians are doing to us. They know that we are hungry, so they have left their camp and hidden in the open country, saying, ‘They will come out of their city, and we will capture them alive. Then we will enter their city.’”
One of his servants answered him, “Let them take five horses from those left here among all Israel, and let them go there and see.”
They took two horse-drawn chariots, and the king of Israel sent them to pursue the king of Syria. He said to them, “Go and see.”

They went and pursued them as far as the Jordan River. They found the whole road full of clothes and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their panic. Those who had been sent returned and reported to the king of Israel.
The people went out and plundered the Syrian camp. A measure of wheat was sold for one shekel, as the Lord had said, and twice that amount for one shekel.
The king sent the attendant on whose arm he leaned to stand at the gate. The people crushed him at the gate and trampled him, and he died, as the man of God had foretold when they sent him to him.

It happened as Elisha had told the king: two measures of barley for one shekel, and a measure of wheat for one shekel. He had told him, “Tomorrow at this time they will be sold at the gate of Samaria.”

The king’s officer answered him, saying, “Even if God made the channels of heaven pour out grain, what you say would not happen.” Elisha said to him, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not taste it.”
And so it happened: the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.

Elisha said to the woman whose son he had brought back to life, “Get up and go, you and your household, and live where you lived before, for God is sending a famine upon the land.” After this, a famine came upon the land for seven years.
The woman got up and did as Elisha had told her. She went to the land of the Philistines and lived there for seven years.
After seven years had passed, the woman came back from the land of the Philistines. She went and appealed to the king about her house and her fields.
The king questioned Gehazi, the son of Elisha, the man of God, and said to him, “Tell me all the wonderful things Elisha has done.”

While he was telling the king how Elisha had brought a dead child back to life, the woman whose child Elisha had brought back to life came and appealed to the king about her house and her fields. Gehazi said to him, “My lord the king, here is the woman, and here is her child whom Elisha brought back to life.”

The king asked her, and she told him. The king assigned one of his eunuchs to her and said to him, “Restore to her all her property and all the produce of her fields from the day she left her land until now.”
Elisha went to the region of Damascus. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was ill, and they reported to him, saying, “The man of God has come here.”
He said to Hazael, “Take a gift with you and go to meet the man of God. Ask him for the word of God concerning whether I will recover from this illness.”

Hazael went to meet him, taking a gift with him from all the good things of the region of Damascus, with forty camels carrying [?]. He went and reached him and said to Elisha, “Your son Ben-hadad, king of Syria, has sent me to you, saying, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’”
Elisha said to him, “Go and tell him, ‘As for recovering, you will not recover.’ God has shown me that you will certainly die.”
He came before his face, and the man of God was ashamed and wept.

Hazael said to him, “What makes my lord weep?” Elisha said to him, “I know how much you will do to the Israelites. You will burn their cities with fire, kill their brave men with the spear, smash their children, and rip open their pregnant women.”
Hazael said to him, “What am I, your servant, who am like a dead dog, that I should do such a thing?” Elisha said to him, “God has shown me that you will reign over Syria.”
Then he returned from Elisha and went to his master, who said to him, “What did Elisha say to you?” He answered, “He told me, ‘You will certainly recover.’”

Then, on the following day, he took a cloth, dipped it in water, and covered his face with it, and he died. Hazael reigned in his place. In the fifth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.
[And Jehoram, king of Judah,] was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eight years.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, because he married Ahab’s daughter. He did evil before God.
God did not wish to destroy Judah because of David his servant, just as he had told him that he would give his son a lamp for all time.
In his days, Edom rose up and rebelled against Judah, and they appointed a king for themselves.
Joram went up to Shihor with all his chariots. He rose up and struck down the Edomites who had surrounded him and the commanders of their chariots. Then they fled and returned to their homes.
Edom rose up and rebelled against Judah, and remains in rebellion to this day. At that time Libnah also rose up in rebellion.
All the acts of Joram and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
Joram rested with his ancestors in the city of David his father, and his son Ahaziah reigned in his place.
In the twelfth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king.
He was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel for one year. His mother’s name was Athaliah, daughter of Zimri, king of Israel.
He followed the ways of the house of Ahab and did evil before God, as the house of Ahab had done.
He went with Joram son of Ahab to war, to fight Hazael, king of Syria, the Philistines [?], at Ramoth-gilead. The Syrians wounded Joram.

King Joram returned to Israel to recover from the wounds inflicted on him at Ramoth when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. Ahaziah son of Joram went down to see Joram son of Ahab in Israel, because he was ill.
The prophet Elisha called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, “Fasten your belt around your waist, take a horn of oil with you, and go to Ramoth-gilead.
Go in there and look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. Go in, have him rise from among his companions, and take him into an inner room.
Take the horn of oil, pour it on his head, and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord says: I have anointed you to reign over Israel.’ Then open the door and flee without stopping.”
That son of a prophet went to Ramoth-gilead.
He found the army commanders sitting there and said, “I have a message for you, commander.” Jehu said, “For which one of us?” He answered, “For you, commander.”
He rose and went into the house. He poured the oil on his head and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I have anointed you to reign over the Lord’s people, Israel,
so that you may destroy the house of Ahab your master from before me and avenge the blood of my servants the prophets and the blood of all the Lord’s servants at the hand of Jezebel
and at the hand of Ahab’s entire household. You shall destroy the house of Ahab, down to every male who urinates against a wall, everyone confined and everyone remaining among them in Israel.
I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah.
Dogs will eat Jezebel in the territory of Israel, and she will find no one to bury her.” Then he opened the door and fled.
Jehu came out to his master’s men, and they said to him, “Peace to you! Why did this man come to you?” He said to them, “Don’t you know this man and how he raves [?]?”
They said to him, “You are lying! Tell us.” So Jehu said to his men, “He said such and such to me, and he told me, ‘This is what the Lord says: I have anointed you to reign over Israel.’”
When they heard this, they hurried, and all of them spread their garments for him where he was sitting on the steps. They blew a horn and said, “Jehu is king!”
Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi, rose against Joram. Joram was in Ramoth-gilead, and all Israel was guarding him against Hazael king of Syria.

King Joram had returned to Israel to recover from the wounds the Syrians had inflicted on him when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. Jehu said to those with him, “Can you commit yourselves to me? Then keep watch, and let no one escape you or leave your city to bring news to Israel.”

Then Jehu went quickly down to Israel. Joram king of Israel was in Israel recovering from the wounds the pagan Syrians had inflicted on him at Ramoth when he fought against Hazael king of Syria, for he was a strong and mighty man. Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to see Joram.

A lookout climbed into the watchtower to keep watch over Israel. He saw the dust raised by Jehu’s men as they approached and said, “Look, I see dust!” Joram said, “Let a horseman go to meet them and say to them, ‘Peace to you!’”

A horseman went to meet them and said to them, “The king says to you, ‘Peace to you!’” Jehu said to him, “What have you to do with peace? Fall in behind me.” The lookout reported to them, “The man you sent has reached them, but he has not returned.”
He sent another horseman, who reached them and said to them, “The king says, ‘Peace to you!’” Jehu said to him, “What have you to do with peace? Fall in behind me.”
The lookout reported to him, “The man you sent has reached them, but he has not returned. The driving is that of Jehu son of Nimshi, for their manner of traveling is different.”

Joram said, “Come, let us go!” They brought out their chariots, and Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah both went out in their chariots. They went to meet Jehu and found him in the field of Naboth the Israelite.
He said to him, “Peace to Jehu!” But Jehu said to him, “What have you to do with peace? Are not the prostitutions and sorceries of your mother Jezebel many?”
Joram turned to flee and said to Ahaz, “We have been betrayed, Ahaz!”
He took up his bow and drew it with all his strength. He shot Joram between the shoulders, and his arrow came out through his heart. He fell to his knees.

Jehu said to Bidkar his attendant, “Throw him into the field of Naboth the Israelite. For I remember, and you yourself know, when we were riding donkeys and following Ahab his father, the Lord pronounced this against him:
“I saw Naboth’s blood and the blood of his sons yesterday,” says the Lord, “and I will repay him in this vineyard,” says the Lord. “Now take him and throw him into this vineyard, as the Lord said.”

When Ahaziah king of Judah saw this, he fled along the road to Beth-haggan. Jehu followed and pursued him, saying, “I will not spare him either.” He struck him down in his chariot as he went up toward Gai, near Ibleam. From there he fled to Megiddo, and there he died.
His servants carried him in his chariot and brought him into Jerusalem. They buried him in his tomb in the City of David.
Ahaziah became king of Judah in the eleventh year of the reign of Joram king of Israel.
Jehu went into Israel, and Jezebel heard about it. She painted her eyes, adorned herself, arranged her hair, and looked out through the window.
Jehu entered the city, and she said to him, “Peace to Zimri, the murderer of his master!”
He raised his face, saw her in the window, and said to her, “Who are you? Come down here to me.” Then two eunuchs looked out.
He said to them, “Throw her down!” They threw her down, and her blood splashed onto the walls and the horses, and they trampled her.
Jehu went in, ate and drank, and then said, “Go and look after this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king’s daughter.”
They went to bury her, but they found nothing except her skull, the soles of her feet, and the palms of her hands.
They returned and told him. He said, “This is the word of the Lord that he spoke through Elijah the Tishbite: ‘Dogs will eat Jezebel in the vineyard of Israel.
[And Jezebel’s corpse will become] like earth on the surface of the open country in the territory of Israel, so that no one will say, ‘This is Jezebel.’”
Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. [Jehu] wrote a letter and sent it to Samaria, to the officials of Samaria, the elders, and the guardians of Ahab’s sons. He wrote as follows:
Now, as soon as this letter reaches you, look: your lord’s sons are with you, and so are his horses, his chariots, his fortified cities, and his field equipment.
“Choose for yourselves the best of your master’s sons, whichever one you want, and place him on his father’s throne. Then fight for your master’s house.”
They were very afraid and said, “Two kings could not stand against him. How, then, can we stand against him?”

The officials of the palace, the officials of the city, the elders, and their guardians sent word to Jehu, saying, “We are your servants, and we will do whatever you command us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever you wish.”

Then Jehu wrote them a second letter, saying, “If you are on my side and obey my word, cut off the heads of your master’s sons and send them to me in Israel by this time tomorrow.” The king’s sons were seventy men, the leading men of the city.
When the letter reached them, they took the king’s sons and slaughtered them, seventy men. They put their heads into wooden baskets and sent them to him in Israel.
His messenger arrived and told him, “I have brought the heads of the king’s sons.” The king said to him, “Throw them in a heap at the city gate in the morning.”
When morning came, the king went out to the city gate and said to all the people, “You are safe. Look, I rebelled against the house of my masters and killed them. But who killed all these?”
“Look and see that none of the Lord’s word that he spoke against Ahab’s house in Israel will fall to the ground. The Lord has done everything he spoke through his servant Elijah.”
Jehu killed all the people of Ahab’s house who remained in Israel, all his leading men, all his acquaintances, and all his priests. He did not leave even one of them alive.
He set out and went toward Samaria, and he reached Beth-eked, where the shepherds were, along the road.

Jehu met the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah and said to them, “Who are you?” They said to him, “We are the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah. We have come down to ask about the welfare of the king’s sons and the sons of his mighty men.”
He ordered them to be captured alive, and they slaughtered them at Beth-eked, forty-two men. He did not leave even one of them alive.

He went on from there and met Jehonadab son of Rechab on the road, coming to meet him. He greeted him, and Jehu said to him, “Is your heart upright toward me, as my heart is upright toward you?” Jehonadab answered him, “Yes.” Jehu said to him, “If that is truly so, give me your hand.” He gave him his hand, and Jehu brought him up beside him into his chariot.
He said to him, “Come with me and see how zealous I am for the Lord of hosts.” He had him ride with him in his chariot.
He entered Samaria and killed all the people of Ahab who remained in Samaria, until he had wiped them out, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken to Elijah.
Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, “Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much.

Now summon for me all Baal’s prophets, all his servants, and all his priests. Leave no one out, for there is a great sacrifice for Baal, and anyone who does not come will die.” But Jehu was deceiving them so that he could kill all the servants of Baal.
Jehu said to them, “Consecrate your sacrifice to Baal.” And they proclaimed it to them.

Jehu sent throughout all the cities of Israel, and all the servants of Baal and all his prophets came. Not one man among them failed to come. They all entered the temple of Baal and filled the entire temple.
Jehu said to the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out clothing for all the servants of Baal.” He brought out clothes for them to wear.

Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab entered the temple of Baal. He said to the servants of Baal, “Inspect and find out whether any servants of the Lord are among you. You alone must be servants of Baal; at your sacrifice no one else is to be here.”
Jehu ordered eighty men to stand outside and said to them, “If you let even one of these men whom I bring out to you escape, your life will be taken in place of the life of the man you let escape.”

Then, when they had finished offering the sacrifice, Jehu said to his guards and his soldiers, “Go in and kill them. Let none of them escape from you.” They killed them with the sword, and his guards and soldiers threw them out and entered the city.
They burned the temple of Baal, all its furnishings, and all its garments.
They knocked down all the images of Baal.
Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel at that time.
But Jehu did not abandon the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel astray. Jehu did not turn away from those golden calves, one in Bethel and one in Dan.

The Lord said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in my sight and have done to the house of Ahab everything I intended in my heart, your descendants will sit on the throne of Israel down to the fourth generation.”
But Jehu did not take care to follow the law of the Lord, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not abandon the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel astray.
At that time the Lord began to strike Israel, and Hazael struck them throughout all the territories of Israel:
east of the Jordan, throughout the land of Gilead belonging to Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh, from Aroer on the bank of the Arnon, including Gilead and Bashan.
All the deeds of Jehu, everything he did, all his might, and all those he killed are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
Jehu rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz became king in his place.
Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-eight years.
When Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, saw that her son was dead, she destroyed the royal family.

Jehosheba, the daughter of King Jehoram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king’s children who were being killed, along with his nurse. She hid him in an inner chamber from Athaliah, so that she did not kill him.
She kept him hidden for six years, while Athaliah herself reigned over the land for six years.

In the seventh year Jehoiada sent for the commanders of the Carites and the runners and brought them to him in the house of the Lord. He made a covenant of the Lord with them and made them swear an oath before the Lord. Then Jehoiada showed them the king’s son.
He said to them, “Do this: a third of you are to come in on the Sabbath, guard the king’s house, and remain at the gate.”
A third of you are to take your places in the broad streets, toward the gate of the enclosure behind the king’s guards. Guard and secure the house.
The other two divisions of you—all those going off duty on the Sabbath—are to guard the house of the Lord where the king is.
All of you are to surround the king, carrying your weapons. Kill anyone who enters the ranks. Those with the king are to accompany him when he comes in and goes out.
The commanders did everything that Jehoiada the wise man commanded them. Each took his men, and they assembled everyone coming on duty on the Sabbath and went to Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada gave the commanders David’s spears and weapons, which were in the house of the Lord.
His guards stood with their weapons, from the right side of the house to the left side of the house of the altar, and surrounded the king.
They brought out the king’s son, and he dressed him in the garment of [?] of testimony, made him king, and anointed him. They clapped their hands and said, “May the father of the king live!”
Athaliah heard the sound of the people running and came to the people in the house of the Lord.

[?] She found the king standing and leaning against the pillar, as was their custom. Before him they were blowing horns, and there were songs. All the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing horns. Athaliah tore her clothes, cried out, and said, “Treason! Treason!”

Jehoiada the priest commanded the commanders and said to the officers of the army, “Bring her out of the ranks, and kill anyone who follows her with the sword.” For the priest had commanded that they not kill her in the house of the Lord.
They seized her and took her along the horses’ entrance to the king’s palace, and they killed her there.
Jehoiada established a covenant between the house of the Lord, the royal house, and the people, that they should be the Lord’s people.

All the people of the land entered the house of Baal and demolished it. They tore down his altars and completely smashed his images. They killed Mattan, Baal’s priest, in front of the altar. The priest appointed overseers for the house of the Lord.

He took the commanders, the Carites, the runners, and all the people of the land. They brought the king out of the house of the Lord, and he led him through the gate used by the guards to the royal house and seated him on the throne of the kings.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was then at peace. They had killed Athaliah with the sword in the royal house.
Joash was seven years old when he became king.
In the seventh year of Jehu’s reign, Joash became king. He reigned in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother’s name was Abijah, daughter of Beersheba.
Joash did what was right before the Lord throughout the time that Jehoiada the priest instructed him.
However, he did not remove the houses of the gods. The people still burned incense and offered sacrifices there, in the houses of the gods.

Joash said to the priests, “All the gold that people consecrate and bring into the house of the Lord, the gold paid for redemption, and all the gold that anyone willingly brings into the house of the Lord—
let the priests take it for themselves, each man from his own dealings, and let them repair the damage in the house.”
Then, in the thirty-third year of Joash’s reign, when Joash saw that the priests had not repaired the damage inside the house,

King Joash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, “Why have you not repaired the damage inside the house? From now on, do not take the gold for your own dealings. They are to bring it for the repairs inside the house.”
The priests agreed that they would no longer take the gold offered by the people and that they would repair the damage inside the house.

Jehoiada the priest took a chest, bored a hole in its lid, and placed it beside [?], in the house of the overseer of the house of the Lord. The priests put into it all the gold found in the house of the Lord, according to its allotment.

When they saw that there was a great deal of gold in the chest, the king’s secretary and the priests went up, counted the gold, and tied it up, storing all the gold they found in the house of the Lord.

He commanded the overseers of the house of the Lord to take the gold that came in, so that they would have it for expenses and could give it to the carpenters and builders who were building the house of the Lord.
And to the builders and stonecutters, to buy cut stone and hewn timber for repairing the damage in the house of the Lord, and for all the expenses of repairing the house of the Lord.
Except for the silver doors made for the house of the Lord, the bowls, the trumpets, and all the gold and silver articles brought into the house of the Lord.
He ordered that it be given to those doing the work, so that they could repair the house of the Lord with it.
Do not require an accounting from those men who receive the gold and distribute it for their work, for they act faithfully.
The gold brought into the house of the Lord for sin and for repentance belongs to the priests.
At that time Hazael king of Syria went up, fought against Gath, and captured Gath. He gathered his forces, and Hazael sent an army ahead of him to go up to Jerusalem.

Joash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, kings of Judah, had dedicated, together with what he himself had dedicated and all the gold found in the treasury of the house of the Lord and in the king's palace. He sent it to Hazael king of Syria, and Hazael returned and left Jerusalem alone.
All the deeds of Joash and everything he did are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
His servants rose up and conspired against him [?], and they killed Joash in the house of Millo, which is in the wilderness.
Jozacar, Jamuhad, and Jozabad his son were the servants who killed him. He died, and they buried him with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Amaziah became king in his place.
In the twenty-third year of the reign of Joash son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king in Samaria and reigned for seventeen years.
He did evil before the Lord and followed the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel astray. He did not abandon it.
The Lord became angry with Israel and delivered them into the hands of Hazael king of Syria and into the hands of Ben-hadad son of Hazael throughout that time.
Jehoahaz pleaded before the Lord, for he saw Israel's suffering, because the king of Syria was oppressing them.
The Lord sent a deliverer to Israel and brought them out of the hands of the Syrians. The Israelites lived in their homes as before.
Nevertheless, they did not abandon the sin of the house of Jeroboam, who had led Israel astray, but continued to follow it. The sacred tree shrine also remained standing in Samaria.
No forces remained to Jehoahaz except fifty horses, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Syria had killed them all and trampled them like dirt.
All the deeds of Jehoahaz, everything he did, and all his mighty acts are written in the book of the prophets, the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Jehoahaz rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in Samaria. His son Joash became king in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of the reign of Joash king of Judah, Joash son of Jehoahaz became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned for sixteen years.
He did evil before the Lord. He did not abandon any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel astray, but continued to follow them.
All the deeds of Joash, everything he did, and all his mighty acts are written in the book of the prophets, the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
He rested with his ancestors, and another Jeroboam became king and sat on his throne in Samaria among the Israelites.

Elisha was suffering from his ongoing illness, from which he would die. Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept before him, saying, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and their horses!”
Elisha said to him, “Take your bow and your arrow.”
He said to the king, “Take hold of your bow and fit your arrow.” Joash fitted the arrow and held his bow in his hands, and Elisha placed his hands over the king’s hands.

He said to him, “Open the window toward the east,” and he opened it. Elisha said to him, “Shoot,” and he shot. Elisha said to him, “The arrow of the Lord’s deliverance, the arrow of victory over Syria! You will strike down the Syrians from Aphek to the very end.”
Elisha said to him, “Take the bow and shoot into the ground.” The king shot three times and stopped.

The man of God was distressed and said to him, “If you had struck seven times, or at least six, you would have killed the Syrians and finished them off. But now you will defeat the Syrians only three times.”
Elisha died, and they buried him. In that year the Moabites raided their land.

While they were burying Elisha, they brought another man to bury. When they saw the raiders coming against them, they threw that man’s corpse into Elisha’s tomb. The corpse fell [?] upon Elisha, and it touched Elisha’s body. The man came to life, rose, and stood on his feet.
Hazael oppressed Israel throughout all the days of Joash.

The Lord had mercy on them and showed them compassion because of the oath he had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Lord did not wish to destroy them, and he did not cast them away from his presence.
Hazael king of Syria died, and his son Ben-hadad became king in his place.

Joash son of Jehoahaz returned and took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the towns he had taken from his father Jehoahaz. When he fought against him, Joash defeated him three times and took back Israel’s towns.
In the second year of the reign of Joash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan, and she was from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, though not as David his ancestor had done. He did everything as his father Joash had done.
But he did not demolish the temples of the gods. The people still burned incense and offered sacrifices there in the temples of the gods.
When his kingdom was secure, he killed the servants who had killed his father.

But he did not kill the children of those who had killed him, because it is written in the book of the law of Moses, as the Lord commanded: “Fathers must not die for their children’s sins, and children must not die for their fathers’ sins. Each person must die for his own sin.”
He killed ten thousand men of Edom at [?]. He reached their stronghold as he struck them down, and he named it Joktheel, its name to this day.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Joash son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come, let us meet face to face.”

Joash sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thornbush among the trees of Lebanon sent word to the cedar tree in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son in marriage.’ But the wild animals in Lebanon came and killed the thornbush.

Because you have defeated the Edomites, you have become proud. Enjoy your glory and stay at home. Why bring trouble upon yourself through your arrogance, when you and Judah with you are going to fall?”
Amaziah refused to listen. Joash king of Israel went up and met Amaziah king of Judah at Beth-shemesh in the land of Judah, and they faced one another.
Judah fell before Israel, and they fled and went into their homes.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah son of Joash at Beth-shemesh. He entered Jerusalem and hung him on Jerusalem’s fortifications at the Gate of Ephraim, and dragged him as far as the Corner Gate, four hundred cubits.

He took the gold, the silver, and all the articles found in the house of the Lord and in the treasury of the king’s house. He also took the children of the foreigners who had joined him, and returned to Samaria.
All the deeds of Joash, all his might, and how he fought against Amaziah king of Judah are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
Joash rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam became king in his place.
Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived for fifteen years after the death of the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.
All the deeds of Amaziah and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
The people of Jerusalem conspired against him, and he escaped from there to Lachish. The king of Lachish sent after him, pursued him, and killed him there.
They loaded his corpse onto horses and buried him in Jerusalem with his ancestors, in the City of David.
Then all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old at the time, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elam and restored it to Judah after the king had rested with his ancestors.
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash became king over Israel in Samaria. He reigned forty-one years.
He did evil before the Lord and did not abandon any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin.

He restored Israel’s borders from the entrance to Hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, as the Lord, the God of Israel, had said, as he had spoken through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.
For the Lord saw that Israel’s suffering was exceedingly bitter. They had become few and had been abandoned, and there was no one to help Israel.
The Lord had not said that he would wipe out Israel’s descendants from under heaven, and he saved them through Jeroboam son of Joash.

The whole history of Jeroboam, the whole course of his life, all his might, all his warfare, and how he recovered Hamath and Damascus from Israel for Judah—these are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
Jeroboam rested with his ancestors, with the kings of Israel, and his son Zechariah became king in his place.
In the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah, king of Judah, became king.
Azariah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah, and she was from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the sight of the Lord, as his father Amaziah had done.
But he did not remove the temples of the gods. The people still burned incense and offered sacrifices there in the temples of the gods.

The Lord afflicted the king, and leprosy took hold of him until the day he died. He ruled from a separate house, while Jonathan, the king’s son, managed his household and governed the people of the land.
The whole account of Azariah and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
Azariah rested with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Jonathan became king in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of the reign of Azariah, king of Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king over Israel in Samaria for six months.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, as his ancestors had done. He did not abandon the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin.
Shallum son of Jabesh, Balaan, and Shallum his father rebelled against him and killed him. Shallum became king in his place.
The whole history of Zechariah is written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
This was the word of the Lord to Jehu, when he said, “Your descendants will sit on the throne of Israel down to the fourth generation.” And so it happened.
Shallum son of Jabesh became king. In the thirty-ninth year of the reign of Azariah king of Judah, Shallum became king and reigned in Samaria for thirty days.
Menahem son of Gadi went up from Tirzah [?] and went to Samaria, where he killed Shallum son of Jabesh.
The whole history of Shallum, including the conspiracy he carried out, is written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.

Then Menahem struck down Tirzah, everyone in Tirzah, all their surrounding territories, and the territory extending from Tirzah, because they had not opened their gates to him. He killed everyone within it and ripped open their pregnant women.
In the thirty-ninth year of the reign of Azariah, king of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king over Israel for ten years in Samaria.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not abandon any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin.
In his days, Pul king of Persia came up into that land. Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver so that he would ally himself with him.
Menahem commanded Israel to give a large amount of silver to the king of Persia, each man contributing fifty shekels to him. The king of Persia did not come and did not stay in that land.
All the deeds of Menahem and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
Menahem rested with his ancestors.
In the fiftieth year of the reign of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned for two years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not abandon the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel astray.

Pekah son of Remaliah, his officer, rebelled against him and [?] him in Samaria, in front of the king’s house, along with Argob and Arieh. With him were fifty men from among the four hundred. He killed him and became king in his place.
All the deeds of Pekahiah and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
In the fifty-second year of the reign of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned for twenty years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not abandon the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel astray.

In the days of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser king of Persia came and captured Nain, Abel, [?], Janoah, Kenaz, Hazor, Gilead in Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali. He deported their people to the land of Persia.
Hoshea son of Elah conspired against Pekah son of Remaliah, killed him, and became king in his place in the twentieth year of Jonathan son of Azariah.
All the deeds of Pekah and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel.
In the second year of the reign of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham son of Azariah became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok.
He did what was good in the sight of the Lord, just as his father Azariah had done in everything.
However, he did not remove the temples of the gods, and the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense in the temples of the gods. He built the upper gate of the house of the Lord.
The whole account of Jotham and everything he did are written in the book of the [?] of the kings of Judah.
At that time the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Jerusalem.
Jotham rested with his ancestors in the city of David his ancestor, and his son Ahaz became king in his place.
In the seventeenth year of the reign of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.

Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He did not do what was good in the sight of the Lord his God and was not faithful like David his ancestor.
He followed the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, king of Israel, and sacrificed his son in fire according to the abominable practices of the nations whom the Lord had driven out before Israel.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense to them in the temples of the gods, on the hills, and under every leafy tree.
At that time Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up against Jerusalem to fight against its people. They fought against Ahaz but could not defeat him.
At that time Rezin king of Syria restored Elath to Syria and drove the Jews out of Elath. The people of Edom entered Elath and lived there to this day.

Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Persia, saying, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen against me.”
Ahaz took the gold and silver found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the king’s house, and sent them to the king as his gift.
The king of Persia said yes to him. The king of Persia went up to Damascus, captured its people, deported them, and killed Rezin.
King Ahaz went to meet Tiglath-pileser, king of Persia, in Damascus. He saw an altar there in Damascus, and King Ahaz sent Uriah the priest a model of that altar and a plan of all its workmanship.
Uriah the priest built an altar entirely according to what King Ahaz had sent him from Damascus.
The king saw that altar and went up onto it.
He burned incense, offered sacrifices, poured out a drink offering, and poured the blood of the peace offerings onto the altar.
He moved the bronze altar that stood before the Lord away from the front of the house of the Lord, from between it and the altar, and placed it on the south side of the altar.

King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, “On the larger altar offer the morning sacrifice and the evening sacrifice, the king’s offering and his sacrifice, and the sacrifices of all the people, their offerings and their drink offerings. Pour onto it all the blood of the sacrifices and all the blood of their offerings. Let the bronze altar be for us morning by morning.”
Uriah the priest did everything just as King Ahaz commanded him.
The king shut all the panels of the stands and removed the basins from them. He also moved the Sea, lowering it from the bronze oxen beneath it, and made a stone support for it.
He built the foundation of its support in the house of the Lord. He brought the king’s entrance and the outer entrance into the house of the Lord because of the king of Persia.
All the deeds of Ahaz and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
Ahaz lay down with his ancestors, and they buried him in the city of David. His son Hezekiah became king in his place.
In the twelfth year of the reign of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned for nine years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, but not like the kings of Israel who were before him.
Shalmaneser, king of Persia, came up, and Hoshea became his servant and paid him tribute.

The king of Persia was displeased with him because he sent messengers to So king of Egypt and did not bring tribute to the king of Persia that year. The king of Persia fought against him and bound him in prison.
The king of Persia came up throughout the whole land, went up to Samaria, and fought against it for three years.

In the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign, the king of Persia captured Samaria and deported Israel to the land of Persia. He settled them in Halah, in Habor, the rivers of Gozan, and in the mountains of the Medes.

When the Israelites sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt from under the power of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, they did not fear the Lord but worshipped other gods.
They followed the customs of the nations whom the Lord had removed from before the Israelites, and everything that the kings of Israel had done.
The Israelites devised all kinds of things that the Lord their God did not desire. They built temples for themselves in all their cities, from the watchmen’s shelters to the fortified cities.
They made an image for themselves and worshipped it, and consecrated trees on every high mountain and hill and beneath every leafy tree.

There they burned incense in all the temples of their gods, as did the nations whom the Lord had driven out before them. They did abominable things and practiced oppression, provoking the Lord to anger.
They served the gods about which the Lord had told them, “Be careful not to do this.” [?]

The Lord warned Israel and Judah through all his prophets, while they all listened, saying to them, “Turn back from your evil way and keep my ways, my commandments, my judgments, and all my law, which I commanded your ancestors, and everything I sent to them through my servants the prophets.”
They did not listen, but stiffened their backs more than their ancestors had.

They did not keep any of the covenant about which he had warned them. They followed worthless things and became worthless, and they followed the nations around them, although the Lord had commanded them not to act like them.
They abandoned the commandment of the Lord their God and made for themselves cast images, two calves. They made wooden idols for themselves, bowed down to all the host of heaven, and worshiped Baal.
They sacrificed their sons and daughters to them in fire, practiced divination and sorcery, and sold themselves to do evil before the Lord and to provoke him to anger.
The Lord became very angry with Israel and cast them out of his presence. Only the tribe of Judah remained.
But Judah also failed to keep the commandment of the Lord their God. They followed the practices Israel had adopted and abandoned the Lord.
The Lord became angry with all the descendants of Israel. He afflicted them and handed them over to those who plundered them, until he cast them out of his presence.
There was no one from the house of David except Israel [?]. They made Jeroboam son of Nebat king, and he made Israel abandon following the Lord and led them astray into great sin.
The Israelites followed all the sins that Jeroboam committed and did not abandon them,

until the Lord cast Israel out of his presence, just as the Lord had spoken through all his servants the prophets. Israel was deported from their land to the land of Persia, where they remain to this day.

The king of Persia brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ela, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took possession of Samaria, divided it among themselves, and lived in its cities.
At the beginning of their settlement there, they did not fear the Lord. So the Lord sent lions against them, and the lions killed them.

The king of Persia was told, “These nations whom you deported and settled in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the god of that land. He has sent lions against them, which have devoured and killed them, because they do not know the law of the god of that land.”
The king of Persia ordered that they take one priest from among the Jews and send him to live among them and teach them the law of the god of the land.
They took one priest from among those who had been deported from Samaria and settled him in Bethel. That priest taught them to fear the Lord.
Each nation made its own gods and placed them in the temples that the people of Samaria had made. Each nation did this in the cities where they lived.
The people of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the people of Cuthah made Nergal, and the people of Hamath made Ashima.
The people of Avva made Nibhaz, Tartak, and Lephron, where they sacrificed their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
They attached themselves to the Lord, but they placed their gods in the temples of their gods in Samaria, each nation in its own cities.
They feared the Lord while worshiping their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been deported there, and they do so to this day.
They feared him, and they themselves acted according to the laws they taught and according to the law of the Lord and his commandment, which he gave to the descendants of Jacob, whom he named Israel.
The Lord made a covenant with them and commanded them, saying, “Do not fear other gods, bow down to them, worship them, or sacrifice to them.
Instead, fear the Lord, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and an uplifted arm. Bow down to him and sacrifice to him.
Keep all his judgments, his law, and his commandments, which he wrote for you, so that you may carry them out all your days. Do not fear other gods.
Do not forget the covenant he made with you, and do not fear other gods.
Instead, fear the Lord your God, and he will rescue you from all your enemies.”
Do not listen to them concerning their laws, which they practice.
These nations continued to fear the Lord while serving their own gods. Their children and their grandchildren have done as their ancestors did, down to this day.
In the third year of the reign of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign.
He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Abi, daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, in everything just as his father David had done.

He demolished the temples of the gods, broke all the images, and uprooted their sacred groves, as well as the serpent that Moses had made. For until that day the Israelites had been burning incense to it, and they called it Nestali [?], in the Lord, the God of Israel.
He trusted in the Lord, and there was no one like him among the kings of Judah, nor among those before him.
He followed the Lord and did not turn away from him. He kept the commandments that Moses [?] had commanded.
The Lord was with him in everything he did. They rebelled against the king of Persia and did not serve him.
He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its surrounding territory, from the watchtower to the fortified city.
In the fourth year of Hezekiah's reign, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Persia marched against Samaria.
He besieged them for three years. In the sixth year of Hezekiah's reign, which was the ninth year of the reign of Hoshea king of Israel, he captured Samaria.
The king of Persia deported the people of Samaria to the land of Persia and settled them in Halah, in Habor by the rivers of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
This was because they did not obey the voice of the Lord their God. They abandoned his covenant, everything he had commanded Moses, the Lord's servant, and refused to do it.
In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah's reign, Sennacherib king of Persia marched against the great cities of Judah and captured them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent messengers to the king of Persia at Lachish, saying, “I repent of the wrong I have done. Leave me alone; whatever you impose on me, I will bear.” The king of Persia imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah a payment of three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
Hezekiah gave all the gold found in the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king's house.
At that time Hezekiah broke up the doors of the house of the Lord and [?] the supporting bases with their gold, and gave it to the king of Persia.
