The king of Persia sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh from Lachish with a large army to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. They marched up and reached Jerusalem, and stood by the water channel of the upper pool, beside the road to the fuller's field.
They called for Hezekiah, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward, Shebna the secretary, and Jehoshaphat the recorder came out to them.
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah: This is what the great king, the king of Persia, says: What is this confidence you have?
You rely on your words and your counsel, not on strength for battle. Now, in whom have you trusted, that you have rebelled against me?

Now you have trusted in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff. If a man leans on it, it breaks, and a splinter enters his hand and wounds him. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to everyone who relies on him.
And as for your saying, ‘I rely on the Lord my God,’ is he not the one whose temples and altars Hezekiah removed, telling Judah and Jerusalem, ‘Worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?
Now come to my master, the king of Persia, and I will give you two thousand horses. Bring enough men to ride them.
How, then, can you turn back even one official, one of the least of my master's servants? Yet you have trusted in Egypt for chariots and horses.
And now, have we marched into this land to fight against it without the Lord's command? The Lord said to us, ‘March into this land and fight against it.’”

Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Jehoshaphat said to the Rabshakeh, “Speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew. Why are you speaking within hearing of the people on the wall?”

The Rabshakeh said to them, “Did my master send me to your master to tell him these words? Was it not to these men sitting on the wall, so that they may eat their own excrement and drink their own urine with you?”
The Rabshakeh stood and shouted to them in Hebrew, saying, “Hear the words of the great king of Persia!”
This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you with his words. He cannot save you from my hand.
Do not let Hezekiah make you put your hope in the Lord by saying, ‘The Lord will save you, and the king of Persia will not be able to take this city.’

Do not listen to Hezekiah. This is what the king of Persia says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then all of you will drink your own wine, eat your own figs, and drink water from your own cisterns,

until I come and take you to a land like your own land, a land of wheat, wine, grain, oil, and honey. You will live and not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah, because he is deceiving you and telling you, ‘The Lord will save you.’
Have any of the gods of the nations saved their lands from the hand of the king of Persia?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim? How is it that they did not save Samaria from my hand?
Who among all the gods has saved a land from my hand?
They remained silent and did not answer him a word, because the king had commanded them not to answer him.
Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward, Shebna the secretary, and Joash son of Shaphan, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him what the Rabshakeh had said.
When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the Lord.
He sent Eliakim the steward, Shebna the secretary, and the chief priests, dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
He said to him, ‘Today is a day of distress; this day is a day of testing and punishment. Labor pains have seized the woman giving birth, but she has no strength.’

[?] May the Lord God hear all the words spoken by the Rabshakeh, whom his master, the king of Persia, sent to insult the living Lord, and may he humiliate him for the words that the Lord your God has heard. Pray for us who remain.
The king’s servants arrived before Isaiah.
Isaiah said to them, ‘Tell your master: This is what the Lord says: Do not be afraid because of these words you have heard, the insults spoken by the servants of the king of Persia.’
Look, I will send a spirit upon them. They will hear news and return to their own land, and I will kill them with the sword in their own land.
The Rabshakeh returned and found the king fighting against Libnah, because he had heard that they had driven him away from Lachish.
He heard about Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia. They told him, ‘Look, he has come out to fight against you.’ He turned back and sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying:
‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by telling you, “Jerusalem will not fall into the hands of the king of Persia.”
You yourself have heard everything the kings of Persia have done, and how they destroyed everything on their campaigns.
Did any of the gods of the nations we killed save them, or those my ancestors killed—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the son of Sedeqen [?], who were in Telassar?
Where is the king of Arpad and the king of Hamath? Where are Lefaru [?], Hena, and Ivvah?’
Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers’ hands and read it. He went up into the house of the Lord, and Hezekiah spread it out before the Lord.
He said, ‘Lord, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the world. You made heaven and earth.
Turn your ear toward me and hear me. Open your eyes and see. Hear the words Sennacherib sent to belittle the living God.
For truly, Lord, the kings of Persia have destroyed the nations,
and they burned their gods with fire, because they were not gods. They were the work of human hands; they were wood and stone. So they destroyed them.’
And now, Lord our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kings of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord.
Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah, saying, “This is what the Lord, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, says: I have heard what you prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Persia.”
“This is the word that the Lord has spoken against him: He has mocked you and despised you, daughter Zion, and shaken his head over you, daughter Jerusalem.
Whom have you mocked, and against whom have you raised your voice? Look toward heaven with your eyes, toward the Holy One of Israel, [?] through his angels.

But you have mocked your Lord and said, ‘With my many chariots I will ascend to heaven and into the lofty mountains, the mountains of Lebanon. I have cut down its great cedars and its fine cypresses, and I have reached the middle of the wilderness.
I myself have rested and drunk foreign water, and with the tread of my feet I have dried up every field and the rivers.’
I made it and brought it about, and you were to destroy [?] fortified cities.

The hands of those who lived in them grew weak. They were defeated and put to shame. They became like grass in the wilderness, like green plants, like grass on rooftops, and [?] before your throne was established.
I know your coming in and your going out, and the rage you have directed against me.
Your arrogance has reached my ears. I will put my hook in your nose and a bridle between your lips, and I will turn you back by the road on which you came.
And this is its sign: This year eat the grain that grows by itself, and in the second year what springs up. In the third year sow and reap, plant vines and eat their fruit.
The surviving house of Judah will spread its roots below and bear its fruit above.
For their remnant will go out from Jerusalem, and those who have escaped from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord will do this.

And it is not like him [?]. This is what the Lord says concerning the king of Persia: He will not enter this city, says the Lord. He will not shoot an arrow there, nor bring his weapons near, nor march over its ground.
He will return by the road on which he came, and he will not enter this city, says the Lord.
I will strengthen this city for the sake of David my servant.”
After this, the angel of the Lord went out and killed 185,000 in the Persian camp. When they awoke in the morning, they found them all dead bodies.
They rose, broke camp, and departed. The king of Persia went back and stayed in Nineveh.

While he was worshiping in the house of his god Shadrach, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with a sword. They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon became king in his place.
At that time Hezekiah became sick and was near death. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the Lord says: Put your house in order, for you will die and will not live.”
Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord, praising him:
“Lord, remember how I have walked before you in righteousness and have done what is good with a whole heart.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Isaiah reached the middle courtyard [?], and the Lord spoke to him and said:

“Go back and tell Hezekiah, the king of my people: This is what the Lord, the God of David your father, says: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Look, I myself will heal you. On the third day you will go up to the house of the Lord.
I will add fifteen years to your life and save you from the hand of the king of Persia. I will also strengthen this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”
He said to him, “Take a lump of figs and apply it where you are suffering, and you will live.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “What is the sign that the Lord will restore me to life and that I will go up to the house of the Lord on the third day?”
Isaiah said to him, “This is the sign from the LORD that the LORD will carry out the word he has spoken: should the shadow go down ten steps, or go back ten steps?”
Hezekiah said to him, “Let the shadow go back ten steps.”
Isaiah the prophet cried out to the LORD, and the shadow went back ten steps.
At that time Merodach son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill.

Hezekiah was pleased because of him and showed them his entire treasure house: the gold, the silver, the spices, the fine oil, the storehouse of equipment, and everything found in his treasury. There was nothing in his house or in all his domain that Hezekiah did not show them.

Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and said to him, “What did these men say, and where did they come from to visit you?” Hezekiah said to him, “They came to me from a distant country, from Babylon.”
He said to him, “What did you show them?” He replied, “They saw everything in my house, and they also saw what was in my treasuries.”
Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD.

‘Look, the days are coming,’ says the LORD, ‘when they will take everything in your house and everything your ancestors have stored up until today and carry it away to Babylon. They will leave nothing,’ says the LORD.
‘They will take your sons whom you have fathered and make them eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.’”
Hezekiah said to him, “The LORD has spoken well. Let there be peace in my days.”

All the deeds of Hezekiah, all his mighty achievements, everything he did concerning the pool and the water channel, and how he brought water into the city—these are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
Hezekiah rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in the City of David. His son Manasseh became king in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-five years. His mother’s name was Hephzibah.
He did evil in the LORD’s sight, following the abominable practices of the nations whom the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.

He rebuilt the temples of the gods that his father Hezekiah had demolished. He made an altar for Baal and sacred groves, as Ahab king of Israel had done. He bowed down to all the host of heaven and served them.
He built an altar in the house of the LORD, concerning which the LORD had said, “In Jerusalem I will place my name.”
He built altars for the heavenly host in both courtyards of the Lord’s temple.
He sacrificed his son in fire, practiced divination and sorcery, and appointed mediums and spiritists. He did much evil in the LORD’s sight and provoked him to anger.

He placed the carved image of the sacred grove in the house about which the LORD had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this house in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from among all the people of Israel, I will establish my name forever.
Israel will not again be driven from the land that I gave their ancestors, provided they obey everything I commanded them, which my servant Moses told them.”
But they did not listen. Manasseh led them astray to do evil in the LORD’s sight, and they provoked him to anger more than the nations whom the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke through his servants the prophets, saying:
“Because Manasseh king of Judah has done abominable evil beyond everything the Amorites before him did, and Judah too has sinned along with their servants,
is this not what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Look, I am bringing disaster upon Jerusalem and Judah, so that everyone who hears of it will grasp both ears.
I will apply to Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plumb line of Ahab’s house. I will wipe Jerusalem as a dish is wiped; after it has been wiped, it is turned face down.
I will destroy the remnant of my people and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. Their enemies will take them captive and plunder them.’”
For they have done evil in my sight and provoked me to anger from the day I brought their ancestors out of Egypt until today.

Manasseh also poured out innocent blood, slaughtering people until he had filled Jerusalem from its entrance to its farthest edge, through the sin by which he led Judah astray and committed sin in the sight of the Lord.
All the acts of Manasseh, everything he did, and the sin he committed are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
Manasseh rested with his ancestors and was buried in the garden of the house of Uzza. His son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for two years. His mother's name was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father Manasseh [?] had done.
He followed every path his father had followed. He worshiped the gods his father had worshiped and bowed down to them.
He abandoned the Lord, the God of his ancestors, and did not walk in the way of the Lord.
Amon's sons rebelled against him and killed the king in his house.
The people of the land killed everyone who had rebelled against King Amon, and the people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place.
All the acts of Amon, what he did, are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
They buried him in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah became king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother’s name was Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah, from Basuroth.
He did what was right before the Lord, in his sight, and walked in all the ways of his ancestor David. He did not turn aside to the right or to the left.
In the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, in the eighth month, the king sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the scribe, to the house of the Lord, saying:
“Go up to Hilkiah the high priest and seal up the gold brought into the house of the Lord, which the gatekeepers have collected from the people.
Hand it over to those supervising the work on the house of the Lord, so that they may repair the damage in the house.
For the carpenters, builders, and men doing the work, to buy timber and dressed stone to repair the damage to his house.
They are not to be required to account for the gold given to them, because they work faithfully.”
Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “Read to him.”

He entered the house of the Lord, went to the king, and brought his report back to the king, saying to him, “Your servants have melted down the silver found in the house of the Lord and given it to those doing the work on the house of the Lord.”
Shaphan said to the king, “Hilkiah the priest gave me a book of the law.” And Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king heard that book of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king gave orders to Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying:

Go and plead with the Lord on my behalf and on behalf of all the people of Judah concerning all the words of this book. For the Lord’s great wrath that has come upon us burns like fire. Our ancestors did not listen to the words of this book or obey the laws written in it.

Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the mother of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, the keeper of the garments. She lived in Jerusalem, with her dwelling there in Manasseh, and they spoke to her.
She said to them, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Tell the man who sent you to me:
‘This is what the Lord says: Look, I am bringing disaster upon this land and upon those who live in it—all the words contained in the book that the king of Judah read.
Because you have abandoned me and burned incense to other gods, provoking me to anger with the work of your hands, my wrath will burn in this land and will not be extinguished.’
And to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, say this: ‘This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: This word that you heard:

Because you did not harden your heart, but feared before the Lord when you heard what I said against this land and its inhabitants—that I would destroy them and they would become a curse—and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I myself have heard you, says the Lord.

And is it not so? Look, I will kill you, and you will die and join your ancestors. You will enter your grave in peace, and your eyes will not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this land and its inhabitants.
They brought the message back to the king. Then the king sent for all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem and gathered them before him.

The king went up to the house of the Lord, and all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem went with him, along with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, both small and great. He read before them all the words of the book of the law that had been found in the house of the Lord.

The king stood beside the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord, that they would keep his commandments, his judgments, and his laws with all their hearts and all their souls, to establish their covenant according to these words.

The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, the priests under him, and the gatekeepers to bring out all the objects belonging to Baal, the sacred groves, and all the host of heaven. They took them outside Jerusalem into the fields of Kidron, gathered their ashes, and carried them to Bethel.

He burned the idolatrous priests whom the king of Judah had appointed, who burned incense in the temples of the gods in the cities of Judah and around Jerusalem, as well as those who burned incense to Baal, the sun, the moon, the constellations, and all the host of heaven.

He brought them, together with their gods, out of the Lord’s temple, outside Jerusalem to the Kidron stream. They burned them at the Kidron stream and smashed them, and he put their broken pieces in the graves of the common people.
He tore down the house of the male cult prostitutes that was in the house of the Lord, where women wove for the god [?].

He brought the priests out of the cities of Judah and defiled the temples of the gods where those priests burned incense, from Gebal to Beersheba. He tore down the shrines at the entrances, beside the entrance to the gate of Hosea, the city's governor, on the right side of the city gate, the gate leading toward [?].
But the priests of the gods were not allowed at the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, except when they ate with their companions.
They defiled Topheth in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that every man would sacrifice his son and every man his daughter to Molech by fire.

He burned the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, inside the entrance to the house of the Lord, in the alms treasury of Nathan the eunuch, in Parwarim. He also burned the chariots of the sun with fire.

The king tore down the altars on the roof of the upper room of Ahaz that the king of Judah had made, and the altar that Manasseh had made in the two courtyards of the house of the Lord. He brought them down from there, broke them apart, and threw their broken pieces into the Kidron stream.

The king defiled the temple facing Jerusalem, to the right of the Mount of Corruption, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians, for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom, the unclean god of the Ammonites.
He smashed their images, cut down their sacred groves, and filled their sites with human bones.

He also tore down the altar at Bethel, at the temple of their gods, which Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel astray, had made. He demolished that altar of their god's temple, broke it apart, crushed its stones, ground them up, and burned their sacred grove.

Josiah went and saw the graves in that city. He sent men, and they brought out all the bones from those graves. He burned them on the altar and defiled it, according to the word of the Lord spoken by the man of God on the day of the festival that Jeroboam held. Then he turned and saw the grave of the man of God who had spoken these words.
He said to them, “What is this tomb that I see?” The people of that land told him, “It is the grave of the man of God who came from Judah and spoke these words concerning the altar at Bethel.”
He said to them, “Leave him alone. Let no one disturb his bones.” So his bones were preserved, together with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.
Josiah tore down all the temples of their gods in Samaria that the kings of Israel had established to provoke the Lord to anger. In each temple he did everything he had done at Bethel.
He sacrificed all the priests of the gods who were there on their altars, and they burned human bones there. Then he entered Jerusalem.
The king commanded all the people to celebrate the Passover of the Lord their God, as written in that book of the law.
For such a Passover had not been celebrated since the days of the judges who judged Israel, throughout all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.
But in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, the Passover of the Lord was celebrated in Jerusalem.

Josiah removed the mediums, the diviners, the household gods, all their gods, and all the shameful things they had made in Judah and Jerusalem, to fulfill the words of their law that were written in the document that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the Lord.

Among the kings before him there was none like him who turned to the Lord with all his heart, all his strength, and all his soul, in accordance with the whole law of Moses. Nor did anyone like him arise after him.
Nevertheless, the Lord did not turn away from his anger against Judah, the anger that Manasseh had provoked.
The Lord said, “I will also remove Judah from before my face, just as I removed Israel. I will destroy this city, Jerusalem, which I chose, and this house of which I said, ‘My name will be there.’”
All the affairs of Josiah and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
In his days Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Persia at the Euphrates River. Josiah went to meet him, and Neco killed him at Megiddo when they met.

His servants transported his dead body from Megiddo and brought him to Jerusalem, where they buried him in a tomb. The people of the land took his son Jehoahaz, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done.

Pharaoh Neco deported him to Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he would not reign in Jerusalem. He imposed tribute on their whole country and ordered them to pay one hundred talents of gold and one hundred talents of silver.
Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim, the son of Josiah, king of Judah in place of his father Josiah, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz and brought him to the land of Egypt, where he died.

Jehoiakim gave Pharaoh his gold and silver. He had his whole country assessed so that they would pay tribute in gold to Pharaoh. Each man paid tribute to Pharaoh Neco according to the amount of his wealth.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Jeldaph, daughter of Pedaiah, [?] Rumah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done.
In his days Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up into that country, and Jehoiakim served him for three years. Then he turned against him and rebelled.

The Lord sent the forces of Syria, the forces of Moab, and the forces of the Ammonites. He sent them into the land of Judah to subjugate its people, just as the Lord had spoken through his servants the prophets.
Nevertheless, the Lord's anger was against Judah, to remove it from before his face because of the sins of Manasseh and everything he had done.
He killed an innocent person and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the Lord refused to forgive them.
All the affairs of Jehoiakim and everything he did are written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Judah.
Jehoiakim lay down with his ancestors, and they buried him in the garden of Uzza. His son Jehoiachin became king in his place.
The king of Egypt no longer went out from his country, because the king of Babylon had taken everything belonging to the king of Egypt, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother's name was Nehushta, the daughter of Elnathan, who was from Jerusalem.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done.
At that time Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up to Jerusalem. The city was fortified, and they fortified themselves.
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came to the city with his troops to fight against them.

Jehoiachin, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon with his children, his messengers, and his palace officials. The king of Babylon seized him and took him away in the eighth year of his reign.

He brought out all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king’s palace, and broke up all the gold vessels that Solomon king of Israel had made for the house of the Lord, just as the Lord had said.
He deported Jerusalem, all their officials, their leading men, and their mighty warriors—ten thousand captives in all—and all their craftsmen and carpenters. He left no one except the poorest people.
He deported Jehoiachin to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his eunuchs, and the leading men of the land. He deported them all to Babylon.
The king deported all their military officers, seven thousand men, and their craftsmen and carpenters, one thousand—all strong men capable of fighting. He deported them all to Babylon.
The king of Babylon made Nethaniah, his father’s brother, king in his place. He changed his name, calling him Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah.
He did evil before the Lord, just as Jehoiakim had done.
For the Lord’s anger came upon Jerusalem and Judah until he drove them out of his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his army. He took up a position against it and besieged it.
The city remained under siege until the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign, until the ninth day of the month.
There was a severe famine, and the people of the land had no food.

The city was breached, and all the fighting men went out at night by the road through the middle gate, toward the king’s garden. The Persians had surrounded the city, but the men went out toward the Arabah.
The Persian army pursued them and followed the king. They captured him in the plains of Jericho, and all his men fled and abandoned him.
They captured the king and took him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and he spoke to him.
He slaughtered his sons before his eyes, blinded Zedekiah, bound him in chains, and took him to Babylon.

On the seventh day of the waxing moon in the seventh month, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the king’s chief cook, who attended him, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the house of the Lord, the king’s palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. The king’s captain of the guard burned them.
The Persian armies demolished Jerusalem’s fortifications.
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, deported the people who remained in the city, those who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and everyone else who remained, to Keram and Erebi [?].
The captain of the guard left some of the poorest people of the land to tend vineyards and cultivate the soil.
The Persians broke up the bronze pillars of the house of the Lord, the stands, and the bronze Sea belonging to the house of the Lord, and carried their bronze to Babylon.
They also took the pots, the [?], the bowls, and all the bronze utensils used in the service.
The captain of the guard took the censers and bowls made of gold and silver.
The two pillars, the single basin called the Sea, and the stands that King Solomon had made for the Lord’s temple—the weight of their bronze could not be measured.

Each pillar was eighteen cubits tall, with a bronze capital on top. The capital was three cubits high, with pomegranates on the capital and one [?], all of bronze. The second pillar was the same, with a hundred flowers on the latticework around it.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah his son, who was his deputy, and the doorkeepers.

From the city he took one eunuch who was an officer over the fighting men, six men who attended the king and were found in the city, the military officer’s secretary who gave orders to the people of the land, and sixty men of the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
The king of Babylon killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath. And Judah was deported from their land.
Over the people who remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left behind, he appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan.

All the military commanders and their people heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, and they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Pethite, and Ozniah son of Maacath, together with their men.
Gedaliah swore an oath to them and their men and said to them, “Do not be afraid of the Persians. Stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you.”

In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, who was of the royal family, came with ten men. He killed Gedaliah, who died, and also the Jews and the Persians who were with him in Mizpah.
All the people, small and great, and their army commanders rose and went to the land of Egypt, because they were afraid of the Persians.

In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin king of Judah had been deported, on the twelfth day of the waning moon in the tenth month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon honored him. In the first year of his reign, he honored Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison.
He spoke kindly to him and raised his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon.
He dressed him in fine clothes, and he always ate with him.
He received all his daily provisions from the king’s household, and they gave them to him each morning throughout his life.
